i-4.7-close-project.title: 4.7 Close Project or Phase: administrative closure, contract closure, transition, final report
i-4.7-close-project.notes: Finalise all activities for the project, phase or contract; key benefits: information archived, planned work completed, team resources released; performed once or at predefined points. The PM reviews the plan to confirm all work is done and objectives met. Administrative closure activities: satisfy exit criteria (documents and deliverables up to date, issues resolved, delivery and formal acceptance confirmed by the customer, all costs charged, accounts closed, personnel reassigned, excess material handled, facilities and equipment reallocated, final reports produced); contractual completion (confirm formal acceptance of seller work, finalise open claims, update records, archive); collect records, audit success or failure, manage knowledge sharing and transfer, identify lessons learned, archive; transfer products to the next phase or operations; send suggestions for improving organisational policies to the right unit; measure stakeholder satisfaction. Also establishes procedures to investigate and document reasons if the project is terminated early. Inputs: charter (success criteria, approval requirements, who signs off); plan (all components); documents (assumption log, basis of estimates, change log, issue log - check none open, lessons learned register - finalised, milestone list, project communications, quality control measurements, quality reports, requirements documentation, risk register, risk report - check no open risks); accepted deliverables (from 5.5; may include partial deliverables for phased or cancelled projects); business documents (business case - did expected outcomes occur; benefits management plan - were benefits achieved as planned); agreements (formal procurement closure requirements in contract terms and the procurement management plan); procurement documentation (collected, indexed and filed: schedule, scope, quality and cost performance, change documentation, payment records, inspection results, as-built drawings, manuals - used for lessons learned and evaluating contractors); OPAs (closure guidelines incl. audits, evaluations, product validations, acceptance criteria, contract closure, resource reassignment, team appraisals, knowledge transfer; configuration management knowledge base). Tools: expert judgment (management control, audit, legal and procurement, legislation); data analysis - document analysis (lessons and knowledge sharing), regression analysis (interrelationships between project variables that contributed to outcomes, to improve future projects), trend analysis (validate organisational models), variance analysis (improve organisational metrics by comparing plan to result); meetings (confirm acceptance, validate exit criteria, formalise contract completion, evaluate satisfaction, gather lessons, transfer knowledge, celebrate; close-out reporting, customer wrap-up, lessons learned, celebration meetings). Outputs: project document updates (all finalised; final lessons learned register covering benefits management, business case accuracy, life cycles, risk and issue management, stakeholder engagement); final product, service or result transition (handover to the group that will operate, maintain and support it - or intermediate result for phase closure); final report (summary description; scope objectives, criteria and evidence of completion; quality objectives, criteria, verification and milestone dates, variance reasons; cost objectives, acceptable range, actuals, variance reasons; validation summary; schedule objectives and whether benefits were achieved, with estimates for future realisation; how business needs were met; risks and issues and how handled); OPA updates (project documents, operational and support documents, project or phase closure documents - formal completion and transfer, reviewing prior phase documentation and customer acceptance from Validate Scope; for terminated projects, why terminated and how finished and unfinished deliverables are transferred; lessons learned repository). Data flow (Figure 4-15, verified): inputs from 4.1 (charter), plan, documents, 5.5 (accepted deliverables), 12.1 (procurement documentation), 12.2 (agreements), business documents and OPAs; outputs to the customer (final product transition), project documents (lessons learned register) and the enterprise (final report, OPA updates).

s-scope-overview.title: Project Scope Management overview: six processes, product vs project scope, predictive vs adaptive scope, requirements, business analysis
s-scope-overview.section: 5 intro, key concepts, trends, tailoring, agile considerations (Figure 5-1)
s-scope-overview.notes: Ensure the project includes all the work required, and only the work required; mainly defining and controlling what is and is not included. Processes: 5.1 Plan Scope Management (scope management plan for defining, validating, controlling scope); 5.2 Collect Requirements (determine, document, manage stakeholder needs and requirements); 5.3 Define Scope (detailed description of project and product); 5.4 Create WBS (subdivide deliverables and work into smaller manageable components); 5.5 Validate Scope (formalise acceptance of completed deliverables); 5.6 Control Scope (monitor scope status and manage changes to the scope baseline). Product scope = features and functions characterising the product, service or result; project scope = the work performed to deliver it (sometimes viewed as including product scope). Completion of project scope is measured against the project management plan; completion of product scope against the product requirements. Requirement = a condition or capability required to be present to satisfy an agreement or formally imposed specification. Predictive: deliverables defined at the start, changes progressively managed; Collect Requirements, Define Scope and Create WBS done early and updated through integrated change control; Validate Scope with each deliverable or phase review; Control Scope ongoing; scope baseline = approved scope statement + WBS + WBS dictionary, changed only via formal change control. Adaptive/agile: detailed scope defined and approved per iteration; overall scope decomposed into a product backlog; team pulls the highest-priority items it can deliver; Collect Requirements, Define Scope and Create WBS repeat each iteration, and so do Validate Scope and Control Scope; sponsor and customer representatives continuously engaged; backlogs (requirements, user stories) reflect current needs. Verified deliverables from Control Quality feed Validate Scope, which yields accepted deliverables signed off by the authorised stakeholder, who should be involved early. Trends: collaborating with business analysis professionals to determine problems and needs, recommend solutions, elicit, document and manage requirements, and facilitate implementation; requirements management starts with a needs assessment (portfolio, program or project) and ends with requirements closure (transition to the recipient to realise and sustain benefits); if a business analyst is assigned, requirements activities are that role's responsibility, while the PM ensures requirements work is in the plan, on time, on budget and delivering value - a collaborative partnership. Tailoring: knowledge and requirements management systems and reuse, validation and control policies, development approach, stability of requirements (unstable areas may need lean/agile until stable), governance. Agile: with evolving requirements, high risk or uncertainty, agile spends less time defining scope up front and more on a process for ongoing discovery and refinement; prototypes and releases close the gap between stated and real business requirements; scope is defined and redefined; requirements constitute the backlog. ITTOs for 5.1-5.6 recorded in ittos.json from Figure 5-1.

s-5.1-plan-scope.title: 5.1 Plan Scope Management: scope management plan and requirements management plan
s-5.1-plan-scope.notes: Create a scope management plan documenting how project and product scope will be defined, validated and controlled; key benefit: guidance on how scope will be managed; performed once or at predefined points. Begins with analysis of the charter, latest approved subsidiary plans, historical information (OPAs) and EEFs. Inputs: charter (purpose, high-level description, assumptions, constraints, high-level requirements); plan (quality management plan - quality policy shapes scope management; project life cycle description; development approach - waterfall, iterative, adaptive, agile or hybrid); EEFs (culture, infrastructure, personnel administration, marketplace); OPAs (policies and procedures, historical information and lessons learned). Tools: expert judgment (previous similar projects, industry/discipline/application area information); data analysis - alternatives analysis of ways to collect requirements, elaborate scope, create the product, validate and control scope; meetings (PM, sponsor, selected team members and stakeholders, owners of scope processes). Outputs: scope management plan - processes for preparing the scope statement, creating the WBS from the detailed scope statement, approving and maintaining the scope baseline, and obtaining formal acceptance of completed deliverables; formal or informal, broad or detailed. Requirements management plan (some call it a business analysis plan) - how requirements activities are planned, tracked and reported; configuration management activities (how changes are initiated, impacts analysed, traced, tracked, reported, and authorisation levels to approve); prioritisation process; metrics and rationale; traceability structure reflecting attributes captured in the traceability matrix. Data flow: charter from 4.1 and plan components in; both plans out to the project management plan.

s-5.2-collect-requirements.title: 5.2 Collect Requirements: elicitation techniques, requirements documentation, traceability matrix
s-5.2-collect-requirements.notes: Determine, document and manage stakeholder needs and requirements to meet objectives; key benefit: the basis for defining product and project scope; performed once or at predefined points. The Guide does not address industry-specific product requirements. Success depends on active stakeholder involvement in discovering and decomposing needs and on care in determining, documenting and managing requirements. Requirements are quantified, documented needs and expectations of sponsor, customer and other stakeholders, detailed enough for the scope baseline and to be measured during execution; they are the foundation of the WBS, and cost, schedule, quality planning and procurement are based on them. Inputs: charter (high-level description and requirements); plan (scope management plan, requirements management plan, stakeholder engagement plan - to adapt to stakeholders' participation level); documents (assumption log, lessons learned register - effective elicitation techniques especially for iterative/adaptive work, stakeholder register - who can provide requirements); business documents (business case - required, desired, optional criteria); agreements (may contain project and product requirements); EEFs (culture, infrastructure, personnel administration, marketplace); OPAs (policies, historical information). Tools (part 1): expert judgment (business analysis, elicitation, analysis, documentation, previous projects, diagramming, facilitation, conflict management); data gathering - brainstorming; interviews (formal or informal, prepared and spontaneous questions, individual or multiple participants; useful for confidential information); focus groups (prequalified stakeholders and SMEs, trained moderator, conversational); questionnaires and surveys (many respondents quickly; varied audiences, quick turnaround, geographically dispersed, statistical analysis); benchmarking (compare products, processes and practices with comparable internal or external organisations to find best practices, ideas and a performance basis); data analysis - document analysis (agreements, business plans, process/interface documentation, business rules repositories, current process flows, marketing literature, problem/issue logs, policies, regulatory documentation, RFPs, use cases); decision making - voting (unanimity: everyone agrees; majority: more than 50%, an odd group size avoids ties; plurality: largest block decides even without a majority, used with more than two options), autocratic (one person decides for the group), multicriteria decision analysis (decision matrix with criteria such as risk, uncertainty, valuation to rank ideas); data representation - affinity diagrams (classify many ideas into groups), mind mapping (consolidate individual brainstorming into one map showing commonalities, differences and new ideas). (Continued in batch B08.) Data flow (Figure 5-5, verified): inputs from 4.1 (charter), plan, documents, business documents, 12.2 (agreements), enterprise; outputs requirements documentation and RTM to project documents.
